title: Of cruelty
hookLine: Montaigne hated cruelty, even to animals (Essays 2.11)

lines: A CRY AT THE EDGE OF A FIELD.
cards: A thin, high cry from the edge of a field: a hare, caught in the dogs' teeth. Montaigne calls the chase a violent pleasure. And in the very same breath, he says he can hardly bear to hear that cry.

The same chase, the same dogs, and a man who can't quite enjoy the ending. He doesn't resolve the tension. He tells the truth about both, and that honesty sets the tone of his essay called Of Cruelty.

teach.b: First, the vice he hates most. Among all the vices, Montaigne writes, he cruelly hates cruelty, by nature and by judgment, as the extreme of them all. Notice the joke: he hates it cruelly.
The one harshness he allows himself is toward cruelty itself.

teach.h: A CHICKEN, A HARE, A DOG.
teach.b: Second, the small creatures. He can't watch a chicken's neck being wrung without discomfort. He can't stand the hare's cry.
And he admits, a bit sheepishly, that his nature is so tender that when his dog offers him a game at the wrong moment, he can't say no. Third, the courts and the wars.
Even in justice, he says, anything beyond plain execution seems to him pure cruelty.
His own time is full of shocking examples, because of the lawlessness of the civil wars: people tormenting others for nothing more than the pleasure of watching. He saw it near home, and he names it.

teach.h: A DUTY TO ALL THAT LIVES.
teach.b: There's a kind of respect, he says, a general duty of humanity, that ties us not only to animals, which have life and feeling, but even to trees and plants.
We owe justice to people, and kindness and gentleness to other creatures that can receive it. He doesn't turn this into a rulebook. He doesn't tell anyone what to eat or whether to hunt.
He draws one line, around unnecessary pain, and it starts small: the spider, the dog, the tone of voice.

how: Readers of Montaigne often take Of Cruelty as a short, practical ethic: refuse needless pain, toward people first, and extend gentleness to animals and living things.

o: a soldier's memoir of battles in the French civil wars
Montaigne's essay: cruelty is the worst vice, even to animals
a defense of harsh punishment as the root of all justice

s: Montaigne says the chase gives no pleasure
he calls the chase a violent pleasure, and still could hardly bear the hare's cry. he tells the truth about both.
he says a duty of humanity ties us even to trees and plants
justice to people, kindness to creatures, and some respect even to trees and plants.
he says punishments beyond plain execution are fair for terrible crimes
he says anything beyond plain execution seems to him pure cruelty.

games.q: you're Montaigne, busy at your desk, and your dog drops a toy at your feet and looks up. what do you do?
o: send the dog away; you're working.
games.why: he admits his nature is so tender that he can't refuse his dog a game, even when it's offered at the wrong moment.

practice: If there's an animal near you, a pet, a bird outside, a fly on the window, watch it for a while; if not, bring one to mind. Notice that it has life and feeling, as Montaigne put it, and let your attention rest on it softly.
Then let one gentle thing come to mind that you could do for a creature, like carrying the spider outside or filling the water bowl.

wordCard.voice: Of cruelty. Montaigne hated cruelty above every vice, and said we owe kindness and gentleness even to animals, and some respect to trees and plants. Today's word.

orig.note: French, from Of Cruelty: I cruelly hate cruelty.

carryVoice: Your line: no cruelty. Gentleness reaches the hare and the dog, too. That's today, done.
